prompt.1: Should food factories be allowed on some weaker farmland in the Fraser Valley?
prompt.2: The province proposed letting food processing plants build on some lower-quality protected farmland. What should happen?
prompt.3: The province proposed letting food plants use some lower-quality land in the Agricultural Land Reserve. What should happen?
prompt.4: A July 2026 proposal would let food processors use Class 5 to 7 reserve soil, up to 0.25% of private reserve land. What now?
prompt.5: The July 2026 proposal would let food processors build on Agricultural Land Reserve Class 5 to 7 soil, capped at 0.25% of private reserve land, with a 5% local-product minimum. Which approach?

context.1: Much of the Fraser Valley is protected farmland that can only be used for farming. The province wants to let food factories build on some of the weaker soil, so more food can be made nearby. Farm groups say the land would be lost.
context.2: Much of the Fraser Valley is in the farmland reserve, where building is limited to farm use. In July 2026 the province proposed letting food processing plants build on lower-quality reserve soil, with a cap on the area and a lower local-content rule. Business groups support it; the farmland commission and farm groups oppose it. The election paused the decision.
context.3: On July 23, 2026 the NDP government proposed letting food processors build on Agricultural Land Reserve land with poorer soil, capped at a small share of private reserve land, with the local-product minimum cut from 50% to 5%. The province says 500 to 1,000 hectares in the Lower Mainland and Fraser Valley could qualify. The Abbotsford Chamber and food manufacturers back it; the Agricultural Land Commission and the BC Agriculture Council oppose it. The election paused the decision.
context.4: The July 23, 2026 proposal would allow food processing on Agricultural Land Reserve Class 5 to 7 soil, cut the local-product minimum from 50% to 5%, and cap the total at 0.25% of the 2.1 million hectares of private reserve land. The province says the soil test excludes about 90% of Fraser Valley farmland and that 500 to 1,000 hectares could qualify. Food manufacturers, the Board of Trade and the Abbotsford Chamber support it. The Agricultural Land Commission and the BC Agriculture Council oppose it. Consultation closed September 18 and the election paused the decision. Eby calls it a food security measure; the Conservatives' October 18 platform does not address it but would remap the reserve and loosen the on-farm processing rule.
context.5: The July 23, 2026 proposal would let food processors build on Agricultural Land Reserve Class 5 to 7 soil, cut the local-product minimum from 50% to 5%, and cap the total at 0.25% of the 2.1 million hectares of privately owned reserve land. The province says the soil condition would exclude about 90% of Lower Mainland and Fraser Valley reserve farmland and 500 to 1,000 hectares could qualify. Supporters include BC Food and Beverage, the Board of Trade and the Abbotsford Chamber of Commerce. The Agricultural Land Commission called it one of the most significant policy shifts in decades; the BC Agriculture Council supports food processing but opposes the proposed rule changes. Consultation closed September 18, 2026 and the election call paused the decision. Eby says it affects 0.3% of the reserve; the Agriculture Council's figure is far larger and the two do not reconcile.

prompt.2: Highway 1 widening is funded to Abbotsford and only planned east of there. Where should the next transportation money go?
prompt.3: Highway 1 widening is funded to Highway 11 in Abbotsford by 2031 and only planned to Chilliwack. Where should the next money go?
prompt.4: Highway 1 widening to Highway 11 is funded ($2.65 billion, due 2031); the Chilliwack phase is not. What should be funded next?
prompt.5: Phase 3B of Highway 1 ($2.65 billion, due 2031) is in procurement; Phase 4 to Chilliwack is unfunded and the 2024 West Coast Express promise has no plan. What next?

context.1: The main highway through the valley is being made wider, but only as far as Abbotsford. Traffic is heavy and buses and trains are few. Parties disagree on whether to keep widening the highway toward Chilliwack, or spend the next money on buses and trains.
context.2: Highway 1 is being widened through Langley and Abbotsford, with work funded as far as Highway 11 and due 2031. The section through Sumas Prairie to Chilliwack is only being planned, with no money or date. In 2024 the government promised commuter rail to Chilliwack but has published no plan. Parties disagree on whether roads or transit should come next.
context.3: The province has funded Highway 1 widening to Highway 11 ($2.65 billion for the latest phase, due 2031). The final phase through Sumas Prairie to Chilliwack is in planning with no funding. The NDP has made no 2026 transport pledge for the valley. The Conservatives pledged six lanes to Chilliwack in 2024, nothing new since. CentreBC names Chilliwack widening in its transport plan. The Greens want transit and rail. OneBC has no position.
context.4: Phase 3B (Mount Lehman Road to Highway 11) is budgeted at $2.65 billion with completion in 2031, on top of $2.34 billion for Phase 3A, now under construction. Phase 4 through Sumas Prairie to Chilliwack is 'in integrated planning' with no funding or date. The NDP's 2024 platform promised West Coast Express service to Chilliwack and new valley rail; by March 2025 there were no details. The NDP has no 2026 valley transport pledge; it rules out a TransLink vehicle levy and said in 2024 there would be no mobility pricing. The Conservatives pledged six lanes through Chilliwack and no tolls in October 2024 and have no 2026 highway or transit commitment. CentreBC names Chilliwack widening and rapid buses in its plan.
context.5: Phase 2 ($345 million) and Phase 3A ($2.34 billion, approved fall 2023) are under construction; Phase 3B (Mount Lehman Road to Highway 11) was funded at $2.65 billion in August 2024 for completion in 2031; Phase 4 (Highway 11 through Sumas Prairie to Chilliwack) is 'in integrated planning' with no funding or date. The NDP's fall 2024 platform promised West Coast Express service to Chilliwack and a new valley rail service; by March 2025 there were no details and it was absent from the minister's mandate letter. The NDP rules out a TransLink vehicle levy (October 2, 2026) and said in 2024 there would be no mobility pricing. The Conservatives pledged six lanes through Chilliwack and no tolls on October 3, 2024; their 2026 plan page has no highway item. CentreBC's $15 billion three-year plan names widening to Chilliwack. The Greens' October 9 plan and October 13 platform fund buses and a passenger rail strategy that names the Fraser Valley. OneBC has no transportation commitment.

context.1: The emergency room at Mission's hospital has often closed overnight this year because there were not enough doctors. People had to drive to Abbotsford instead. Other valley hospitals are very busy too. Parties disagree on the fastest way to keep emergency rooms open.
context.2: Mission Memorial Hospital's emergency room cut overnight hours for 51 nights in a row earlier this year, and closed more nights through the summer, because it could not staff enough doctors. The health authority says it is recruiting, and a bigger emergency room is being built for 2027. Candidates in Abbotsford-Mission debated the closures in September. Parties disagree on what to do first.
context.3: Mission Memorial's emergency room ran reduced overnight hours for 51 straight nights earlier in 2026 and more in the summer, because of physician staffing. Fraser Health says it is recruiting, and an $18 million expansion is due in spring 2027. The Conservatives announced a $50 million fund for rural emergency rooms on October 5. CentreBC promises a law reporting every closure and a yearly fund. The NDP offers tuition discounts and moving costs for rural work.
context.4: Mission Memorial Hospital's emergency department ran reduced overnight hours for 51 consecutive nights earlier in 2026, with further closures through September; Fraser Health cites physician staffing and says it is recruiting. An $18 million emergency department expansion began in February 2026 and is due in spring 2027. The Conservatives' first health announcement was a $50 million fund for rural practices at risk of closing. CentreBC would cut unplanned closure hours in half by 2029/30 and legislate public reporting. The NDP's October 9 plan offers tuition discounts, loan forgiveness and moving costs for rural posts and fast-tracks international graduates. context.5: Mission Memorial Hospital's emergency department ran reduced overnight hours for 51 consecutive nights earlier in 2026, with 16 more closures scheduled for August and September; Fraser Health cites physician staffing and is recruiting. An $18 million expansion began in February 2026 and is due in spring 2027. At the September 14 Abbotsford-Mission debate, candidates from four parties addressed the closures. Party pledges: the Conservatives' $50 million rural practice fund and flexible staffing (October 5); CentreBC's Emergency Room Accountability Act, halved unplanned closure hours by 2029/30, $25 million a year stabilization fund and permanent retention bonus; the NDP's rural tuition, loan forgiveness and moving support, 1,000 training seats and international graduate bridging (October 9); the Greens' community health centres, funding for safe nurse-to-patient ratios and a review toward one health authority; OneBC's private care alongside public and nurse reinstatement.
